rationale: A wins because it is more disciplined about uncertainty and does not confuse a pitchable tension with a proven thesis. Its line, "Without at least the time period, this angle is a bare number and should not be pitched," is the kind of guardrail that saves a founder from walking into a reporter's follow-up empty-handed. B is useful, especially the service angle, but "Patagonia puts a repair counter in every US store" invents a physical retail setup the update does not give us.
gaps_in_A: "A company with no shareholders is giving away repairs — nobody else can copy the math" overstates the ownership point. The update says privately held and profits directed to environmental causes; it does not prove no shareholders or that no competitor can copy the economics.

"Patagonia will now fix your jacket in every US store" risks implying in-store repair. The update only says customers can drop items off at stores; A correctly asks later whether repairs happen on-site, but the headline gets ahead of the fact.

A dismisses "Patagonia customers can now mail in their gear for free repairs" as a duplicate. As B shows, there is a legitimate consumer-service version if the proof includes pricing, shipping, and turnaround.
gaps_in_B: "Patagonia puts a repair counter in every US store" is not grounded. The facts say drop-off at 70+ stores, not counters, in-store repair, or staffing at every location.
"Patagonia's newest store rollout has nothing new to sell" leans too hard on "no new apparel line announced." Absence from this update is not evidence of a deliberate no-new-product strategy.

"what it costs to staff 70-plus locations for it" implies a staffing model the update does not supply. B later asks whether repairs are shipped centrally, but the earlier framing has already wandered.
The next step jumps to "journalist-fit-check" even though the set itself admits missing timeframes, prior-state details, and external pegs. Newsworthiness should be checked before matching reporters.
